You already do this some other way.

A chat app, an automation you built, somebody you pay, or an evening and a GitHub repo. Here is where each of those is the better answer, and where it isn’t.

Every price on these pages was read from the other company’s own pricing page, and dated. Each page carries its own Checked date, the most recent being August 24, 2026; a figure older than 90 days fails our own build check rather than sitting here quietly going stale.

Every assistant we could source

Ten assistants on privacy and control, placed from what their own pages say.

Privacy here means where the work happens: on their servers, or on your computer. Control means whether it checks with you before the steps that matter. Those two are what this site is built around, and every mark is placed by what a company says in public about itself, so “doesn’t say” means exactly that, never that the product cannot. Read September 16, 2026.

Where the other nine beat Archie

Hermes, OpenClaw and Vellum run on your own computer, cost nothing to keep and are open source, and if free and open is how you are choosing, they win it. Vellum makes almost the same custody claim we do, in almost the same words, and reaches a phone, a browser and a terminal besides. Muse and Symphony each have a free plan that renews every month, and ours does not.

What a drawing leaves out

No drawing shows the distance between installing something and having it do your actual job: the accounts wired up, the rules that match how you work, and somebody to ask when it breaks. That gap is what the six comparisons below are about, and it is the honest place to argue with an agent you could run yourself for nothing.

Sources for every mark above
1Archie: custody and what it asks

Our own Trust page, claim by claim, with the code behind each one.

2Archie: the price

Our own pricing page.

3Vellum: runs locally by default, and asks until you mark an action trusted

Read from vellum.ai on September 16, 2026. “By default, your assistant runs locally. Your conversation history, memory, and credentials stay on your machine and are never used to train models.” And: “High-stakes actions like sending emails to new contacts, modifying important files, or spending credits require explicit approval until you mark them as trusted.” The page also says Vellum is open source and is “native to Mac and accessible everywhere: iOS, Android, web app, voice, email, Telegram, Slack, and terminal.”

4Vellum: free to start, then $30, $100 or $200 a month

Read from vellum.ai/pricing on September 16, 2026. “Vellum is free to download and start.” The paid plans are Mighty at $30, Super at $100 and Ultra at $200 a month, each described as a computer of a given size; Mighty is a “Small computer 1 vCPU / 2 GiB, 10 GB storage”. Usage beyond a plan is metered in credits at “$1 = 1 credit”. We do not say where a paid Vellum plan executes, because Vellum does not say.

5OpenClaw: on your machine, and free

Read from openclaw.ai on September 16, 2026. “Mac, Windows, or Linux. Bring hosted, subscription-backed, gateway, or local models. State lives on your machine, not a vendor cloud.” And: “No subscription. No hosted tier. No token.” OpenClaw “is stewarded by the OpenClaw Foundation, an independent US 501(c)(3) non-profit” and is MIT licensed. It reaches “WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, Signal, iMessage, or any of its 29 channels.” The page says nothing about approval before it acts, which is why that cell says so rather than guessing.

6Hermes: desktop or cloud, free and MIT

Read from hermes-agent.nousresearch.com on September 16, 2026, the Nous Research page for it. It offers a desktop app for macOS 12+, Windows 10/11 and Linux, and “Deploy to the cloud” through Nous Portal. It is “free and open source under the MIT license”, and Nous Portal plans run from $0 to $200 a month for credits and hosted services. It reaches “Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Email, CLI”. Nothing on the page addresses approval before acting.

7Claude Cowork: Anthropic’s servers, and a mode that does not ask

Read from Anthropic’s own Cowork guide on August 20, 2026. Cowork’s work “runs on Anthropic’s servers, in an isolated environment, and your sessions and files are saved to your Claude account”. It has three permission modes; in Skip mode “Claude doesn’t pause to ask and nothing checks its actions automatically”.

8Claude Cowork: included from Pro up, $20 a month

Read from claude.com/pricing on August 19 and 20, 2026: “Includes Claude Cowork” on the Pro card, and Pro at $20 a month, or $17 a month billed annually.

9Grok Bot: a persistent cloud VM

Read from x.ai/news/introducing-grok-bot and the Grok Bot overview on August 20, 2026. Each Grok Bot “runs on a persistent cloud VM with a browser, filesystem, and terminal” and signs in to your tools there; it comes back “when something needs your approval”.

10Grok Bot: which plans carry it

Plan cards read in a browser at x.ai/bot on August 20, 2026, because x.ai refuses automated requests: SuperGrok Heavy at $300 a month and Cursor Ultra at $200 a month, with Cursor Teams Premium at $120 a seat also carrying it. No script of ours can re-confirm this one, so it is re-read by hand.

11Meta Muse: a dedicated cloud computer, free for most

Read from Meta’s own announcement on September 15, 2026. Muse “runs on its own dedicated computer in the cloud, contained so no one else’s agent can reach it”, and is “free for most of what people need, with subscription plans for people who want to do more”.

12Meta Muse: what it will not do without approval

Read from Meta’s help centre on September 15, 2026: “By default, Muse will not take many important actions, like sending an email, without your approval.”

13Wix Symphony: how you reach it

Read from wix.com/symphony on September 11, 2026. Symphony is used with a Wix account, in a browser or its iOS and Android apps, and Wix publishes no program you run on your own computer. Where the agents themselves run is not stated on that page, the pricing page, the support overview or the launch release, so this board says Wix does not publish it rather than guessing.

14Wix Symphony: it checks first

Read from Wix’s own overview on September 11, 2026: Symphony “checks with you first before your agents act, so nothing important happens without your approval”.

15Wix Symphony: the plans

Read from wix.com/symphony/pricing on September 11, 2026: a free plan with no credit card needed, then Basic at $16 a month, Pro at $40 and Max at $80, cheaper billed annually. The free plan’s daily credit cap was 50 when we first read this page in August and is 100 now, which is worth knowing against anything written earlier, ours included.

16Instinct: in private access, and publishing little

Read from instinct.com on September 16, 2026. “Instinct is a personal assistant that understands what you’re working on and what’s important to you.” It “connects to your applications and devices - email, messaging, screen, audio, location, and more”, and “It’s trained to use a phone and a computer. You can text or call it.” It is “currently available to a private access group as we’re scaling up compute”. The page gives no price, no statement of where it runs and nothing about approval, which is a fair thing to report and not a fair thing to fill in. Other companies have written about what Instinct does; we do not print those claims, because a competitor writing about a competitor is not a source.

17Norton Family Assistant: asks first, and prices nothing

Read from us.norton.com/products/family-assistant on September 16, 2026. It “keeps your family organized, so you never miss to-dos, calendar events, and important updates in your life”, “Plugs into the apps your family already uses”, and “Asks first, acts after”. Norton says “Your chats are never shared, sold or used to train AI.” The product page carries no price and does not say where it runs.

How these are written

Every page says where the other option wins.

A comparison with no losses in it is an advertisement, and you would be right to read it as one. So each of these carries a section naming what the alternative does better, every price is read from that company’s own pricing page and dated on the page, and every figure links to where it was read so you can check it yourself.
